subject: Distance sampling + genotyping individuals from scats

messages.author: da1b54e297a1f0fd
messages.subject: Distance sampling + genotyping individuals from scats
parts:
Hi all,

I am looking at using distance sampling of scats: the scats are collected along line transects (usually 1km), and extracted DNA is used to identify individuals and therefore "recaptures", between and within transects - thus preventing repeated counts of the same individuals. We are able to extract viable DNA from about 30-40% of collected samples. We are confirming DNA degradation rates in scats experimentally and suspect it is about 3 weeks. Is this design (ie incorporating the scat "recaptures") possible using a distance sampling analysis, and if so, any advice or initial pointers in the right direction for information would help me a lot...

Regards,
Martin.

messages.author: 8fbbf490c07a1909
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Distance sampling + genotyping individuals from scats
parts:
Hi Martin & list

I’m not sure if it’s been tried, but what if for every individual on a transect you divided by the number of scats it produced and used that value in the cluster size column.  So if there were three records of an individual on the transect the ‘cluster size’ (effectively a multiplier) for the three entries for that individual would be 0.33. 

I’m not sure what effect that would have on the variance - it might be useful to check section 2.1.4 of the distance book to see what it says about independence of samples. 

You would probably have to ignore scats that were unable to be identified as they would not be accounted for in this method.  But it has the advantage that it might sidestep the need to know exactly what the lifespan of the scats was because that would be included in the probability of detection.

Roy had a thought that you could use SECR which might be able to extract more from the recapture information. 

Cheers

Stewart

messages.author: 1fb54f491646a589
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Distance sampling + genotyping individuals from scats
parts:
I agree that secr is well worth considering.  But if you're going to use distance sampling, I would not be concerned about how many animals were sampled.  Instead, I would use indirect methods:  treat the scats themselves as the individuals, and estimate scat density.  To convert this to animal density, you would need to estimate the average number of scats an animal produces a day, and the mean time to decay of a scat.  Trying to convert sampled scats to number of animals detected will not work in a distance sampling context, because movement of animals over the period that the scats are available for detection will cause bias, and there is no guarantee that an animal 'on the line' will be detected by this means.  secr can use this additional information though.

Steve Buckland

Martin:

You might notice from the variability in responses you have received to your question, that we're not quite sure how to respond.  There is theory in which "detectors" in SECR (related to distance sampling) are transects.  A variant of that approach uses "cues" which can be faeces attributable to an individual via DNA.

I have only a limited understanding of this, but some of the ideas regarding analysis are presented in the attached PDF that forms a vignette from the R package secr by Murray Efford.
